narrative:
The model estimates that, if admitted, you would have a 56% chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. Because that is more likely than not, the university denied your application.

The strongest factor was your LSAT score. Your score of 20 is far below the admitted-student average of about 37, and it pushed the prediction firmly toward failure. This was the decisive reason for the denial.

Next, your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 was slightly below the average of 3.23 among admitted students, but in this model it actually pushed toward passing. So your GPA was not a cause of the denial; it was a small point in your favor.

The third most important factor was your first-year class rank. You were in the bottom 10% of your class, while admitted students typically sit around the 6th decile. This early academic standing pushed toward bar-exam failure, a warning sign that admissions committees take seriously.

If you wish to reapply, your clearest path is to raise your LSAT score substantially through focused preparation. Strengthening your academic record, perhaps through additional coursework or better study strategies, would also help. Improving these areas could change a future decision in your favor.
